label: bm-open-hardware-repro
topic: Reproducibility pack: parts list, files and costs
summary: Reproduction pack for the first bilayer swelling experiment on Formlabs hardware, with prices read from official Formlabs store pages on 2026-11-12. Bought new, the core kit costs about $9.0k to $11.5k: $5,133 is read directly from Formlabs and Adafruit pages (Form 4 Basic $2,625, Form Wash V2 $699, Form Cure V2 $999, two extra tanks $238, three 1 L resins $547, two humidity sensors $25), $3.4k to $4.7k comes from search-result snippets (mostly the 0.1 mg balance at $2.8k to $3.7k) and $0.4k to $1.7k from unverified guesses. Most of it can be borrowed (printer, wash, cure, balance, scanner, microscope, camera); the unavoidable purchases are resin, tanks, IPA, sensors, salts and small items, about $920 to $1,230. It contradicts an earlier file on one point: Open Material Mode has an official price, $875 for the Form 4, not about $3.7k. It amends the design: a 90 %RH salt jar is not a clean fixed point, so use NaCl (75 %RH) and K2SO4 (about 97 %RH). Instrument needs follow from the signal: a 40x4x1 mm strip weighs about 174 mg, so a 0.1 mg balance gives 0.3 % error at 8 % uptake and a 1 mg balance 2.9 %; length needs optical measurement at about 10 um per pixel with a certified scale, thickness about 2 um pixels. Included: a file-naming and logging convention with a tested validator, a pinned open-source Python stack that resolves under Python 3.14, and SHA-256 manifests of every saved page. The step most likely to differ between labs is conditioning each layer to a defined dry reference mass after the IPA wash: Flexible 80A V2 takes up about 45 % IPA by mass in a day, nobody has measured drying rates, and Formlabs gives two different wash times. PreForm is free but not open source.
lay_summary: This is a shopping list and instruction sheet so another lab can repeat our first test without asking us anything. The test needs a resin 3D printer, a rinse-and-bake station, a very fine scale and a way to hold air at a known dampness. Bought new it costs about as much as a small used car, but most of it can be borrowed from a university lab or makerspace, leaving about a thousand dollars of materials to buy. The step most likely to go differently from lab to lab is getting each printed strip properly dry after its alcohol rinse, because the soft rubber-like resin soaks up almost half its weight in alcohol and nobody has measured how fast it dries. If one lab leaves a trace of alcohol inside, it will read that as the strip swelling in water. So every lab should first record a drying curve, like weighing laundry until it stops getting lighter.

findings.claim: Humidity fixed points of saturated salts at 25 C (Greenspan 1977, Table 2, read from OCR of the NIST PDF): MgCl2 32.78 +-0.16, K2CO3 43.16 +-0.39, Mg(NO3)2 52.89 +-0.22, NaCl 75.29 +-0.12 %RH. K2SO4 is 97.59 (20 C) and 97.00 (30 C) in Table 3, so about 97.3 at 25 C by my linear interpolation.

Salt-jar temperature coefficients from Greenspan Table 3 (20 to 30 C): MgCl2 -0.063, NaCl -0.038, K2SO4 -0.059 %RH per C, so a +-2 C room gives at most +-0.13 %RH; the jar is not the weak link, the sensor is.

DEVIATION from design-biomaterial.json: its 90 %RH jar is not one of the clean saturated-salt points I could read; the readable wet points are NaCl 75 %RH and K2SO4 about 97 %RH. Use those (or log the real RH with a sensor) and call the target RH nominal.

Adafruit SHT45 board is $12.50 with stated accuracy +-1.0 %RH, +-0.1 C, so it cannot separate a 75 % jar from 74 % by itself; the salt jars (+-0.12 to +-0.4 %RH) are the better reference than the sensor.
A 0.1 mg, 220 g analytical balance (Ohaus Pioneer PX224 class) is the largest non-Formlabs cost: US listings in search results ran from $2,805 to $3,747.40; Explorer-class 0.1 mg models $5,700-7,000.

BOM totals (bom.py): all core items bought new $9,016.50-$11,524.24, of which $5,133 is read from Formlabs/Adafruit pages, $3,447.50-4,691.24 from search snippets and $436-1,700 unverified background. Items I flag as commonly borrowable are $8,096.52-10,293.04 of that, leaving $919.98-1,231.20 to buy. Buying only the Formlabs chain new and borrowing the rest: about $5,243-5,554 (own arithmetic).
Resin demand is tiny against the 1 L minimum: total part volume of the planned ~170 strips is 16.9 mL (supports, rafts and tank fill not counted, unknown), 1.7 % of one cartridge.

Balance need: a 40x4x1 mm Flexible 80A V2 strip weighs about 174 mg (1.09 g/cm3). At 8 % uptake (14 mg) a 0.1 mg balance reads uptake to 0.3 % and a 1 mg balance to 2.9 %. At 0.1 % uptake (0.17 mg) even 0.1 mg gives 23 % error; reading 0.1 % to 5 % needs 0.82 g of material on a 0.1 mg balance (8.2 g on a 1 mg one). A 1 mg balance suffices for the swelling candidate, not for proving a passive layer inert on strip-sized coupons.

Length need: 0.2 % strain on 40 mm is 80 um, so the project target of 5 % of that is 4 um; 2400 dpi scanning is 10.6 um/pixel, a 4056-px camera over a 60 mm field is 14.8 um/pixel, a 10 um-step caliper has a difference sd of 4.1 um before contact error on a soft elastomer. So use optical measurement with sub-pixel edge fitting and a certified scale, not callipers; the Flexible 80A V2 1-day strain of about 1 % (400 um) is easy with anything.
Thickness need: 3 % of a 200 um layer is 6 um, so cut-edge images need pixels of about 2 um or finer; callipers cannot do this.

Rough conditioning-time estimate (assumption-laden): with water D >= 6e-12 m2/s (bm-diffusion-kinetics), t90 for a 1 mm slab with both faces open is about 9.8 h and drying about 25 h at 2.5x slower; for 0.2 mm about 0.4 h and 1 h. IPA D is not measured. This conflicts with the minutes-scale scaling (low confidence) in bm-formlabs-printing-workflows.json unless IPA moves much faster than water, so it must be measured as a dry-down curve.

The Python analysis stack resolves together on Python 3.14: numpy 2.5.4, scipy 1.18.1, scikit-image 0.26.0, opencv-python-headless 5.0.0.93, matplotlib 3.11.2, pillow 13.0.0, pytest 9.2.0 (pip --dry-run succeeded; not installed or run, C: is nearly full). recommendations: RUN ORDER FOR A LAB STARTING FROM NOTHING (design says about 5 weeks): (1) install PreForm and record versions; (2) borrow what bom.csv flags Y; (3) buy resin, tanks, IPA, salts, sensors; (4) set up the jars and log RH for 48 h before any specimen goes in; (5) check the balance with check weights and the scanner or camera with a certified scale; (6) run the dry-down curve below before any swelling measurement; (7) then follow agents/design-biomaterial.json.

FOLDER LAYOUT: BM1/PREREG.md; BM1/CAD/ (STL or 3MF per build plus the .form project file); BM1/RAW/<batch>/ (camera DNG, scanner TIFF, edge images, named by naming.py); BM1/LOGS/ (measurements CSV, humidity CSV, one file per day, LF line ends, equipment.csv for printer firmware, PreForm version, resin lot and tank id); BM1/MANIFEST.tsv from naming.py manifest. Git for text files, the manifest for binaries.

FILE NAMES: BM1_<batch P##>_<specimen S### or bilayer B###>_<MASS|IMG|SCN|EDG|RHL|NOTE>_<DRY|R##|H2O|IPA|PRE|WSH>_t####h_<UTC YYYYMMDDTHHMMSSZ>.<csv|json|dng|tif|png|txt>. Example BM1_P01_S003_IMG_H2O_t0024h_20261113T143000Z.dng. Validate with naming.py check; log columns utc,batch,specimen,quantity,value,unit,uncertainty,instrument,operator_code,rh_pct,temp_c,note validated by naming.py log-check.

LOGGING RULES: UTC always; one reading per row; instrument id, operator code, RH and temperature on every row; raw values never overwritten, corrections appended as new rows; every photograph carries the scale target and a grey card in frame.

LENGTH PROTOCOL: scan or photograph at fixed height with the certified scale in the frame; edge position by sub-pixel fit (scikit-image) with a hand cross-check in Fiji on 10 percent of images; callipers only as a gross sanity check on elastomers.

FLAGGED STEP most likely to differ between labs: conditioning each printed layer to a defined dry reference mass after the IPA wash and post-cure (solvent age and time, drying time and RH, and the criterion for constant mass). Why: Flexible 80A V2 takes up about 45 % mass of IPA in a day (data sheet via project record) against 6.9 % for Tough 1000 and under 0.1 % for Rigid 10K; Formlabs prefers fresh solvent for the second wash and rates one IPA refill at 120 prints; the project record has a 10 min versus 5 + 5 min wash disagreement for the same resin; no leaching or drying rate is measured (my estimate is 1 to 25 h depending on thickness). Leftover solvent or leachable monomer would be read as water gain or swelling. Runner-up: UV dose, because a lab without Form Cure V2 will not reproduce the cure. Control: record a dry-down mass curve for 3 strips per resin, define constant mass as under 0.05 % change over 24 h at 22 +-2 C and 33 %RH (my proposed threshold, not from a source), use fresh IPA for the second wash, and log solvent batch and age.

AMENDMENTS TO THE EARLIER DESIGN: wet jar 97 %RH (K2SO4) or 75 %RH (NaCl) instead of 90 %RH; the Flex Build Platform ($339) is optional; Open Material Mode is $875, not about $3.7k, so the hydrogel fallback is cheaper than bm-formlabs-printing-workflows.json said.

IF NO FORMLABS PRINTER IS ACCESSIBLE: ask a makerspace to print the two layers and hand them over unwashed (or washed to your protocol) with resin lot numbers. The Fuse path (about $49.8k before powder) is not realistic to reproduce in-house; keep it as an outsourced option.

PreForm and printer firmware versions: I did not read a current version number from Formlabs; record the versions shown in the app and on the printer with every build. No open-source alternative to PreForm for Form 4 was found.
Which universities or makerspaces hold a Form 4, Form Wash, Form Cure or a 0.1 mg balance: no source. The borrow flags in bom.csv are my judgement, not data.
Whether the Raspberry Pi HQ camera is still in production in 2026-11: unconfirmed (one retailer said production to at least January 2026).
Greenspan Table 2 was read from OCR of a scanned PDF; K2SO4 at 25 C was not readable and is interpolated; check the digits against the page image before citing them.
No source measures bond strength, curl of 0.2-1 mm strips or minimum elastomer wall on Form 4 (carried over unchanged from bm-formlabs-printing-workflows.json); the pilot has to settle them.

glossary.plain: The shopping list: every part, its price and where the price came from.
The liquid plastic a Formlabs printer hardens with light, layer by layer.
Two boxes: one rinses uncured liquid off the part in alcohol, the other bakes it in UV light until it is hard.
Rubbing alcohol at high strength, used as the rinse.
A sealed jar with a salt slurry at the bottom; the air inside settles at a known, fixed dampness.
A very sensitive scale; 0.1 mg is a ten-thousandth of a gram.
The smallest step the scale or ruler can show on its display.
A paid Formlabs unlock that lets the printer use other companies' resins.
The weight of a part once it has dried to a steady, agreed state, so later weight gain can be counted from there.
Writing down what you will measure and what counts as success before looking at the data.
A fingerprint of a file that changes if even one byte changes.
A strip of two stuck-together layers that bends when one layer swells more than the other.
A rubber-like plastic that stretches and springs back.
